Each electron is a little traction engine dragging on the spation lattice; when several share one orbital slot, the ones behind ride in the wake of the ones ahead, and the whole convoy spends less energy per electron. The sky’s quiet glow is microwave. That glow is the packing’s working pressure, still arriving. It is not leftover light from a first day. There was no first day. Light past the Sun is late because it ran slower, not because empty space got longer. Hotter means more pressure. More pressure means far-away light crawls. Climb from the microwave: at the last solid red, then infrared, the far-frame speed has already fallen to a crawl. Solid colour could not move past itself — electromagnetic vibration needs speed. Hard gamma is where through-going light stops. The other way is radio, then a wave as big as the whole stack — not a wave at all, just still. If the bath goes all the way cold, the push that we call gravity shuts off. What was seated spreads. That dump reloads the packing until far-away light cannot move. Then the jam opens. We meet infrared coming down. We sit in the microwave again. When the door opens is not yet a derived date. The order of the climb is.
